assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of magic-angle flat bands in twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity opened the field of moire quantum materials, a clean and original platform for strongly interacting electrons with very broad impact. As a statistical physicist I value that a simple, tunable continuum model organizes a large range of phenomena.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the decisive 2011 theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group delivered the 2018 experimental discovery. This maps naturally onto a theory-plus-experiment prize. Other experimental contributors are outside the supplied credit, so the three-person configuration is defensible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent groups over several years, and the field is still growing. Timing is good: mature enough for a stable interpretation while remaining central.
uncertainties: The microscopic mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated.
Credit among experimental contributors beyond the supplied names is a possible concern; details are from memory and not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Time-reversal-invariant topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect introduced a new classification of band insulators with protected edge states, and reshaped condensed matter physics and materials science. The concepts are original, clear and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction of the Z2 topological phase; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental demonstration in HgTe quantum wells following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the three-dimensional topological-insulator work are not in this candidate's credit, so the allocation is partly incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Very mature: more than a decade of independent confirmation in several materials, with a stable interpretation. Recognition is arguably overdue relative to impact.
uncertainties: BHZ and 3D topological-insulator contributions may need recognition elsewhere, leaving a credit-allocation question.
Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases may count against it for some members.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation of many-body models with ultracold atoms in optical lattices, from the Hubbard-model proposal to its realization, created a controlled laboratory for strongly correlated physics, with impact across condensed matter, statistical mechanics and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Theory credit (Cirac, Zoller, with Jaksch and others not listed) and experimental credit (Bloch, Greiner, Dalibard) are all substantial; five names are supplied, so a three-person set necessarily leaves out important contributors such as Greiner and Dalibard.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with many independent groups and increasingly quantitative benchmarks. Recognition is timely, though the cold-atom prize space is partly occupied by earlier prizes.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should centre on the theory proposal, the Mott-insulator experiment or the broader programme is unresolved.
Cirac and Zoller also appear in the trapped-ion, Rydberg-array and combined-theory candidates, so allocation overlaps.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical discovery of fractional exchange statistics in two dimensions is a deep and original insight linking topology, statistics and quantum many-body physics, and it underpins fractional quantum Hall quasiparticles and topological quantum computing ideas.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim (1977) and Wilczek (1982) are the clear originators within the supplied credit, so the credit is clean, though Wilczek is already a laureate and Halperin and Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek work on quantum Hall statistics are not included here.
assessment.maturity: Experimental anyon exchange statistics were reported only recently (around 2020 onward), so the theory is old but the confirmation is relatively young and still being consolidated.
uncertainties: Interpretation of the recent interferometry and collision experiments is still under discussion.
Overlap with the fractional-quantum-Hall anyon candidate on the experimental side; a combined prize may be preferable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems, the Jarzynski equality and stochastic thermodynamics give exact relations far from equilibrium and a framework for thermodynamics of single stochastic trajectories. This is close to my own field and I see its foundational value, with applications to molecular machines, colloids and small devices.
assessment.attribution: Credit is spread among Evans, Searles, Cohen, Gallavotti, Jarzynski, Crooks, Seifert and others; four names are supplied and a three-person selection is somewhat arbitrary. I choose those with the most general-purpose results, but this is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally verified in RNA/DNA pulling and colloidal systems and theoretically stable. Recognition would be timely, although impact beyond statistical mechanics is more diffuse.
uncertainties: Priority disputes among the early fluctuation-theorem results.
Breadth of impact compared with the leading condensed-matter and quantum candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The defect-mediated theory of two-dimensional melting with a hexatic phase is a classic of statistical mechanics, using defect unbinding and renormalization ideas to describe a continuous melting transition; it has been tested in colloids and simulations.
assessment.attribution: Halperin, Nelson and Young developed the dislocation-mediated melting and hexatic theory following Kosterlitz and Thouless, who were recognized in 2016. The supplied credit is clean, but experimental verification credits are missing.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and stable for decades; the concern is that it may look like a late follow-up to the 2016 prize.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees it as sufficiently distinct from the Kosterlitz-Thouless prize.
Details of the experimental verification are uncertain from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory gave a controlled non-perturbative approach to strongly correlated electrons and, combined with electronic structure, became a workhorse for Mott physics and correlated materials. Its importance and originality are high.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt's infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar's mapping onto an impurity problem, and contributions by Rozenberg and Jarrell are all relevant; the supplied three names cover the core but leave out Metzner.
assessment.maturity: Mature and widely used, though a theoretical method rather than a single discovery, and its predictive success is sometimes qualified.
uncertainties: It is a method more than the discovery of a phenomenon, which may matter for the prize criteria.
Omission of Metzner and others from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Vicsek model and the hydrodynamic theory of flocking established a physical framework for collective motion and helped found active matter, with long-range order in two dimensions as a striking result. This matches my own interests, but I try to evaluate it by prize criteria.
assessment.attribution: Vicsek and coworkers (1995) introduced the model and Toner and Tu the hydrodynamic theory; credit is relatively clear, though Ramaswamy and others contributed to active-matter hydrodynamics.
assessment.maturity: The theory is stable and extensively developed; direct experimental confirmation of the specific exponents is less clean and the field is still evolving, so recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Quantitative experimental confirmation of the Toner-Tu exponents remains limited.
Competing claims from the broader active-matter community.
